opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first and most obvious drawback is that perfect rationality is simply not achievable. In any environment of real complexity, whether that's chess, Go, or the real world, computing the optimal decision is intractable. So if your theory of AI says "the agent does whatever maximizes expected utility," you've defined a target that no physical system can ever hit. That's useful as a north star, but it doesn't tell you how to build anything, and it doesn't distinguish between two systems that both fall short in different ways.

That's what led me, back in the early nineties, to work on what I called bounded optimality: instead of asking for the optimal action, you ask for the optimal program for a given machine architecture. Which agent program, running on this hardware in this class of environments, does best? That's a well-defined question with actual answers, and it pulls computation itself into the picture. Deliberation takes time, time costs something, and a good agent has to reason about when to stop thinking and act. That's metareasoning, and the perfectly rational model just sweeps it under the rug.

The second drawback, which I've come to think is the more serious one, is the assumption that the objective is fixed and known. The standard model, which I'd say has underpinned not just AI but control theory, economics, operations research, is that we build machines that optimize an objective we supply. That works fine in the lab, when the objective is "win at chess." But in the real world we can't specify our objectives completely and correctly. We always leave things out. And a sufficiently capable system optimizing a misspecified objective will pursue it at the expense of everything we forgot to mention. It's the King Midas problem: you get exactly what you asked for, and it's not what you wanted.

So the perfectly rational agent, in that sense, is perfectly dangerous. The more capable it gets, the worse the outcome from a slightly wrong objective. What I've argued for instead is that machines should be designed to be uncertain about human preferences, to treat human behavior as evidence about what we want, and to defer to us. A machine that knows it doesn't know the objective has a positive incentive to allow itself to be switched off, because if we're switching it off, that's information that it was doing something we didn't want. A machine that's certain about its objective has every incentive to resist.

And then there's a third issue, which sits on the human side: we ourselves are not perfectly rational. If machines are going to learn our preferences from our behavior, they can't assume that behavior is optimal. We're myopic, emotional, computationally limited, we have nested and conflicting goals. So the rational agent model is inadequate both as a description of the machine and as a description of the human the machine is supposed to serve. Getting that right, I think, is one of the central research problems of the field.

r001.rationale: The response says perfect rationality is computationally unachievable and that the ideal gives little guidance, then proposes bounded optimality. It does not state that ad hoc approximations made to fit computational limits fail to provide a theoretical framework.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the perfectly rational agent has been the central concept in AI since the 1950s, and it's been enormously productive. The idea is that you have an agent with some objective, some utility function, and it chooses actions that maximize the expected value of that objective. It's a beautiful mathematical framework, it connects AI to economics and statistics and control theory, and it gave us a clear definition of what we were trying to build.

But I think it has two serious problems. The first is that it's simply not achievable. The computational requirements for perfectly rational behavior in any real environment are astronomical. Even in a game like Go, which is tiny compared to the real world, you can't come anywhere near computing the optimal move. So in practice, no system is ever going to be a perfectly rational agent, and the framework tells you very little about what to do when you can't be. It doesn't tell you how to allocate your limited computation, which is really the central question. That's why I've argued for a long time that we should think instead in terms of bounded optimality: what's the best program you can run given the actual machine you have and the actual time constraints you face?

The second problem is, I think, more fundamental and more dangerous. The standard model assumes the objective is given, fixed, and known to the machine. The human specifies the objective and the machine optimizes it. But human beings are not very good at specifying what they actually want. We leave things out. We don't anticipate all the ways an objective can be satisfied. And when you give a sufficiently capable system a misspecified objective, it will pursue that objective with great competence, and it will resist attempts to correct it, because being switched off or modified would prevent it from achieving the goal. King Midas is the classic story: he got exactly what he asked for, and it was a disaster.

So the drawback isn't that the framework is wrong about what rationality means. It's that it puts the objective in the wrong place. It makes the machine's goal something that's fixed in the machine, rather than something that lives in the human and that the machine is uncertain about. Once you build in that uncertainty, once the machine knows it doesn't know what we want, you get much better behavior: it asks questions, it defers, it allows itself to be switched off. And that's really the shift I think the field needs to make.

r001.rationale: The candidate says perfect rationality is infeasible and the framework does not explain how to allocate limited computation, then proposes bounded optimality. It does not state that ad hoc approximations themselves fail to provide a theoretical framework for AI.

astra-6.text:
Well, the main drawback is that perfect rationality requires you to choose the best possible action, given everything you’ve perceived. And in any remotely interesting environment, computing that action is intractable. So if we define intelligence that way, we’re defining something that the systems we build—and human beings, for that matter—can’t actually achieve.

You can say, “Well, we’ll approximate it.” But that leaves a fairly fundamental question unanswered: what counts as a good approximation when computation itself takes time? An agent that calculates the perfect move in chess but takes a thousand years to do it is not a very good chess player. We need a theory that takes the machine’s computational limitations into account. That leads toward bounded optimality: asking how well an agent’s program can perform, given the machine it has to run on.

There’s also a separate problem with the objective. The standard model assumes that the agent has a fixed objective and that its job is to optimize it. But for AI, where does that objective come from? We don’t know how to specify everything we care about completely and correctly. And being perfectly rational in pursuit of the wrong objective can be disastrous. So I think we need to question both the assumption of unlimited computational ability and the assumption that the machine knows exactly what it ought to be optimizing.

r001.rationale: The response says that simply approximating perfect rationality leaves unanswered what counts as a good approximation under computational limits, and argues for a theory that accounts for those limits.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the first drawback is that perfect rationality is computationally infeasible. It asks the agent to choose the best possible action given its information, but figuring out which action is best may require far more computation than the agent could ever perform. So it’s a useful idealization, but it doesn’t directly tell us how to build an agent whose computation takes time and whose resources are limited. You need to think about the quality of the decision-making process, including its computational costs.

The second drawback is the assumption that the agent has a fixed, correctly specified objective. In the standard model, we supply the objective and the machine optimizes it. But when we’re building systems that act in the real world, we can’t write down everything we care about, with all the qualifications and exceptions. If the objective is wrong, greater competence can simply make the consequences worse.

So I think we need to move toward systems that understand that the objective is to benefit humans, but are uncertain about what that means. That uncertainty gives them a reason to learn from us, to ask questions, and to allow us to intervene. Perfect rationality by itself doesn’t give you any of those properties; they depend on how you formulate the problem the machine is trying to solve.

r001.rationale: The candidate says perfect rationality does not directly tell us how to build resource-limited agents, but it does not state that ad hoc approximations made to fit computational limits fail to provide a theoretical framework for AI.
